#5304. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Baljević said two hidden liabilities are data distribution rights for public training datasets used upstream and the evaluation, stability and legal audit costs that shift directly to the enterprise. “When using open-weight models, you need to lean in on understanding data distribution rights, copyright, contractual restrictions and consent,” she said. “In most cases, this carries costs.”

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” said Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any company, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”

In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss said. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”

#5303. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5301. FHFA Increases Conforming Loan Limit by $22k for 2027

The Federal Housing and Finance Authority (FHFA) has announced a new conforming loan limit (the maximum dollar amount for a conventional mortgage) for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mortgages in 2027. The new limit for one-unit properties will be $855,400, up $22,650 from 2026’s limit.

The Housing and Economic Recovery Act (HERA) requires FHFA to adjust the Enterprises’ baseline conforming loan limit each year to reflect the change in the average U.S. home price, according to a release. As the organization’s research found that home prices were up 2.72% on average from Q3 2025 to Q3 2026, the FHFA said that the conforming loan limit has increased on the same baseline.

In addition, high cost areas (where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline conforming loan limit) have a higher limit due to HERA, according to a release. The high cost area limit sits at a ceiling of 150% the baseline limit, which in 2027 will be $1,283,100.

The FHFA also noted special statutory provisions establishing different loan limits for Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the baseline loan limit and the ceiling loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100 and $1,924,650, respectively.

Due to rising home values, the FHFA stated that the conforming loan limit will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents.

Click here for additional information and lists of limits by county.

#5300. How the Kennedys Spent Thanksgiving at Their Hyannis Port Compound—Where JFK and His Father Plotted a Presidential Run

When John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house.

Joseph P. Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat.

Five years earlier, it was what happened after Thanksgiving dinner that the family would remember. John, then a Massachusetts senator, slipped into the study off the living room with his father.

He had a list of reasons to think twice about running for president. Joseph had an answer for every one.

By the time they emerged, the Kennedys had a campaign to plan.

The house where that conversation took place began as a summer rental. In 1926, Joseph and his wife, Rose, brought their children to Malcolm Cottage, a waterfront home overlooking Nantucket Sound. John was just 9.

According to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum, Joseph bought the property two years later for $25,000 and expanded the house to accommodate his growing family.

John eventually bought a place of his own behind his parents’ home. His brother Robert and sister-in-law Ethel came to own an adjoining property.

Together, the three residences formed the 6-acre compound, an arrangement that put several generations of Kennedys within walking distance of Thanksgiving dinner at the Big House.

In "White House by the Sea," author Kate Storey describes a family with surprisingly little use for a formal seating plan. Joseph and Rose took opposite ends of the mahogany table.

Everyone else picked a spot. Family cook Ziptha Anderson remembered far less flexibility when it came to carving the bird.

“They all like the same thing—the white meat,” she said.

The weather had a say in the menu, too. A chilly Thanksgiving called for clam broth, while a mild afternoon meant tomato juice to start.

Dinner was at 1 p.m. in Storey’s account of the 1956 gathering, which still left the family time for Mass and a sail before they made their way to the table.

By Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay, then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children.

One family outing took the president and several of his siblings to the skating rink in Hyannis named for their late brother, Joseph Jr. John watched while Ted and his sisters rented skates and played tag on the ice.

Back at the compound, Bobby and Ted also got a touch football game going. That evening, the adults sat down to Vermont turkey, candied sweet potatoes, and their choice of pies.

Ted found another way to work up an appetite in 1979. A United Press International photographer caught the senator waving from his boat as he took relatives and friends sailing off Hyannis Port before Thanksgiving dinner.

Ethel carried on hosting Thanksgiving at Hyannis Port long after her children had families of their own. In 2010, she enlisted her son Robert to bring home two live turkeys so her grandchildren could see the birds up close. One promptly escaped.

“For three days they chased it everywhere,” Ethel told the Cape Cod Times.

A couple of months later, the newspaper ran a story about a turkey causing trouble in nearby Centerville, where it had even taken on a moving postal truck. Ethel called the newsroom. She thought she knew where the bird had come from.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5299. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:

Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”

For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”

#5298. U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October

U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

Home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

However, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”

There’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

The biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

On a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

The biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

This report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

#5297. Inside a 3-Home Co-Living Compound Designed for Friends To Buy Together

A co-living community in West Oakland, CA, has hit the market for the first time.

The Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995. That’s the asking price for all three homes. If purchased separately by friends, multigenerational families, or any other buyers who want to live side by side, the starting price is $899,000 for the smallest of the three homes, which has five bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound.

This lot has been zoned RM-3, or Mixed Housing Type Residential–3, which allows for multiple single-family homes on a single lot. This setup is permissible due to changes in California law allowing for higher-density housing in residential areas.

This project started in 2019 when a startup called Open Door bought the 7,535-square-foot empty lot and tasked Matt Baran of Baran Studio Architecture with creating a co-living space.

They asked: “What if we design something that can be beautiful design and work with the new state laws that allow for increased density in neighborhoods and works well for community living?” says listing agent Max Nelson, who specializes in co-living sales through the platform Live Near Friends.

The end result was a rent-by-the-room community where residents enjoyed shared amenities, including a backyard fire pit, co-working space, and rooftop deck with views of downtown Oakland.

The design process balanced group-friendly amenities with the look and feel of the neighborhood, which is filled with mostly Victorian homes.

Nelson says that the architects asked, “How do we create a modern house without making it look like it doesn't fit?”

The design included bay windows that jut from the homes, mirroring the style of a classic Victorian. Having three separate homes rather than one huge building also matched the aesthetic of the area, as did the incorporation of tall, narrow windows.

Much of the rest of the design leans more modern, especially the efficient energy systems. The homes rely on shared solar panels, greatly reducing energy bills. Everything is electric—there is no reliance on gas. Each room has its own fan coils to create customized comfort.

“It’s a super efficient, well-done system,” says Nelson.

Because The Union was designed for co-living, some of the best features are the shared spaces and the flow among the three homes.

The property fronting the street, 1514, has the smaller price tag at $899,000 and offers 1,919 square feet of living space, including five bedrooms and four bathrooms. A skybridge connects it with the back two condos, positioned side by side like a duplex and sharing a common wall.

The larger of the back condos, 1510, is listed at $1,049,500 and sits slightly larger at 2,033 square feet, again with five bedrooms and four bathrooms. Connected is 1512, also offered at $1,049,500 with 2,015 square feet, including four bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Above these two condos is the roof area, which houses the solar panels as well as the communal deck with AstroTurf and several seating areas.

It all adds up to a highly functional, thoughtfully designed compound that meets the needs of communal living. It offers both shared spaces as well as smaller decks, outdoor seating nooks, and private spaces for solo or one-on-one time with another—because shared living works best when people have the freedom to come together or enjoy time apart.

#5296. What Next-Gen Real Estate Leaders Are Leaving Behind and Embracing Instead

Above, from left, Eric Fite, Jack Markham, Marisela Harper, Lori Muller and Adrian Provost

“All the technology in the world doesn’t matter unless it makes a fundamental impact on the relationship with the client, the way we serve them. That’s our true north.”

That was the sentiment summed up by Eric Fite, COO of CENTURY 21 Judge Fite Company in Dallas/Fort Worth, when moderating a recent panel of up-and-coming brokerage leaders about what old ways they are leaving behind and what innovative new approaches they are bringing to the fore.

AI and technology and how they can best be used dominated the discussion, but panelists also shared some of the ways they are reimagining traditional business practices to support their agents in the session titled, “Next-Gen Leaders and Their Powerful New Approach to Business,” held this past October at RISMedia’s CEO Exchange in Washington, D.C.

In addition to Fite, the panel included Marisela Harper, broker/owner of ClearView Realty; Adrian Provost, CEO of ONE Terminus & LEVEL; Lori Muller, president of Fathom Realty; and Jack Markham, chief marketing officer at Inside Real Estate.

The group also shared insights into how they are positioning their tech stacks and CRMs, how they are viewing their data and data ownership and control,as well as the future of AI and how it can assist agents through automation.

“I think everybody’s realizing that the CRM is not necessarily your tech stack,” said Markham when asked what old beliefs most forward-thinking brokerages have already abandoned. “Traditionally, you would pick a CRM, and that’s where your data is; that’s who owns the workflows. But quite honestly, the smartest brokers are realizing that the tech stack is way more than your CRM.

“Most teams are running two to three CRMs. And that’s not because everybody loves using multiple CRMs. They do it because it’s a fear of loss. They do it because if I drop a tech stack, if I drop a tool, I don’t want to lose my data. And so they’re doing it as insurance. So I think most of the smart brokers today are realizing they don’t need more tools in the tech stack. They don’t need another tool, another app. What they need is something to absorb the tech stack, something that’s going to empower their data so their agents think less about where they log in and more about how to drive conversations.”

Provost said he views the “tech stack,” or the set of software tools, apps and technologies a company uses, as more of a folder, and a platform as more of an operating system.

“Ultimately, what I look for is how (tech) helps close certain loops that lead to that appointment-to-close loop, and then to that close-to-repeat-and-referral-business. I think that if it’s something that isn’t touching one of those or enhancing the agent’s ability to perform, then it probably doesn’t really belong in the tech or in the platform.”

Fite then turned the conversation to AI, asking panelists how they are using it and consumer behavior data to identify when and how an agent should engage a consumer.

“With consumer behavior data, that data is your opportunity,” Muller said. “It’s your opportunity to be strategic with what you’re going to do with it, how you’re going to utilize it. And then AI is the actual action step. It’s how you take action with that data to create a result.”

Markham said it’s all about control over data.

“The uncomfortable question for most brokers is, if you decided to leave your tools or your tech stack, could you take your data with you? And the answer most likely for most brokers in the industry is no,” he said. “They find out far too late that they can’t take it with them. Real ownership of data means you control that data no matter what CRM or tech tool you’re using.”

On a question about what work AI should be doing for a human, Provost said:

“I look at it from an operational standpoint. How can AI assist me and my agents in enhancing our service to our clients? And in my case, my clients being the agent. And so I think that humans need to always be in the loop. There should never be one point where they’re disconnected, but it should be streamlined, and we should be able to have AI connect components that don’t normally talk to one another so we can perform better and elevate that entire experience for whoever’s on the opposite end of it.”

Muller added that AI can help with automating transaction management, marketing solutions, social media, communication or “B- and C-level” operational tasks, while leaving more time for the most important aspect of the business—client relationships.

“No matter who tries to destroy the real estate industry, you can’t take the relational side away from the Realtor® and the consumer. AI is not going to do it. Technology’s not going to do it. That’s the most important thing we have to look at,” she said.

How does the next generation of real estate business leaders view traditional ways of supporting agents, or “loving on them,” as the panel discussed?

“We really do everything so strategically to love on the agent, down to when we built our office four years ago,” said Harper. “We built this big hub and we put our offices right where people that come in can see us. And that’s done on purpose. We have our staff completely trained to love on the agent. We also train our mentors to love on the agents. And when I say love, that’s really being intentionally present with them, spending the time to go to their weddings, go to the baby showers, attend the funerals because that’s a time when they really need just someone to be there for them.”

She added, “And one of the most important things on that contact card is the agent’s birthday. And that might seem so silly, but when I open my calendar for the day, I see whose birthday it is and that’s the first phone call I make just to call them and wish them a happy birthday. Of course, we do the birthday cards and the gift card and all of that, but the call just to wish them happy birthday, see how they’re doing, it goes over so well. They absolutely love it.”

Here are some more notable quotes from the session:

What’s most important when an agent leaves the brokerage?

Lori Muller: When an agent leaves, sometimes they leave because they think the grass is greener on the other side, and they get over there and it’s not. So I think it’s super important to have some type of exit strategy when an agent leaves and have a conversation to say, “Hey, what could we have done better? What was the situation that caused you to leave?” And it’s a teaching moment for both people. We also just recently did a comeback campaign where we called agents that have left over the last two years, and we have had almost a 25% return rate.

Are we heading toward a world where technology becomes table stakes and culture, service and execution become the real differentiators?

Jack Markham: I think you could take two people and give them the same tech stack, and what’s really going to separate them is not necessarily the tools that you’re using. It’s once you plug in your data, right? Once you plug in those relationships, once you plug in the trust, once you plug in the consumer behaviors that you’ve been tracking and the history behind that, it becomes your thumbprint. What’s unique and can’t be copied is all the history there. It’s all the relationships, it’s all the trust that becomes your thumbprint. And so that can never really be duplicated.

What’s the one move you would make over the next 12 months to better position your brokerage and your agents for where the industry is going?

Jack Markham: Figure out if you own your data. Meaning if you left today, some of your tools, could you take them with you? And if the answer is no, then I would fix that.

Marisela Harper: I would say just be super, super present because (agents) need that from you, and just show the love. And when I say show the love, I really mean truly say, “I love you.” Sometimes people might know that you love them, but they need to hear it too.

Lori Muller: Embrace your relationship with not only your technology, but your people. Longevity is in the relationship with the people; tech stack and your technology is constantly changing.

Adrian Provost: Move away from tech stacks completely and create platforms. The old days are completely over. Whatever you need, you can literally build it. And so I would move away from being so reliant on a tech stack and subscriptions and actually figure out what it is that your agents need and provide that to them.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5295. BTC Price vs. PCE Shock: 21Shares Warns of $53,250

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

BTC price faces another potential sell-off as it awaits today’s inflation report after weeks of heavy selling. Core PCE is expected to rise 0.3% month over month, while 21Shares puts Bitcoin’s realized price at $53,250. A hotter reading could bring that level closer than we want.

The Binance hack initially sent Bitcoin lower, but the price recovered most of its losses by November 4. The sell-off picked up again afterward, driven by ETF withdrawals, shrinking stablecoin balances, and traders being forced out of leveraged positions.

Core PCE is forecast to rise 0.3% month over month, with annual inflation expected at 3.2%. The figure matters as markets reassess the outlook for interest rates and how much room the Federal Reserve has to ease policy.

🇺🇸8:30 AM ET COULD GET EXPENSIVE FOR OVERLEVERAGED TRADERS.September PCE: 3.6%October forecast: 3.8%Core PCE: 3.1% → 3.2% expected.The Fed wants 2%, but inflation is still sitting significantly above that target.If today’s numbers surprise lower, risk assets could… pic.twitter.com/TNuSlaiwx6

Bitcoin has already suffered a sharp reversal this month. The latest drop followed a brief Nvidia-tied recovery that brought BTC back above $60,000, but momentum quickly faded. A hotter inflation reading could put that recovery further out of reach, as Bitcoin is currently struggling to attract sustained buying.

A softer report could help prices recover, but markets are looking for more than a single green candle after several failed attempts to reverse the decline.

Bitcoin Hyper is down to its final day before launch, and the presale price is still low at just $0.0136. That’s the price buyers can get today, with tomorrow’s launch bringing the presale to a close and exchange trading expected to follow.

More than $33.2 million has already gone into the project. That’s a lot of money for a presale, especially with the deadline now just hours away. Buyers also have 35% APY staking rewards on offer, adding another reason some investors aren’t waiting around for the token to hit exchanges.

The timing is what makes this interesting. Tomorrow, the presale price disappears. Anyone planning to buy after launch will have to enter through the market, where the price could move either way. If demand carries over from the presale, waiting could cost buyers a cheaper entry.

$0.0136 is the presale price today, not tomorrow. With $33.2 million raised and launch just around the corner, anyone still considering HYPER is running out of time.

21Shares puts Bitcoin’s realized price at $53,250, based on Glassnode data from November 22. The figure tracks the average value of Bitcoin based on the price at which coins last moved on-chain.

Bitcoin falling toward that level would put more holders underwater. The firm also outlined a deeper scenario near $43,800, a potential 18% drop below realized price. It considers that outcome less likely, given the institutional presence and spot Bitcoin ETFs that were missing during earlier bear markets.

The report also points to fading demand and forced liquidations as major contributors to BTC price decline. The Binance hack may have triggered the initial selloff, but 21Shares argues that the subsequent weakness was driven by deteriorating market demand.

Bitcoin now needs to reclaim $60,000 and hold it. Otherwise, $53,250 could become the next level as the market searches for a floor.

#5294. AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella said that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.8% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

Anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The company thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

#5293. Mortgage applications rise 6.1% even as 30-year hits 7.38%

MBA reported mortgage applications rose 6.1% for the week ending Nov. 20, 2026. Purchase activity led with a 10% gain, while the 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.38% and ARM share increased to 11.5%.  AI Summary

Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026.

On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week.

The refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted purchase index increased 10% from one week earlier. The unadjusted purchase index increased 5% compared with the previous week and was 16% lower than the same week one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks. While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace.”

Kan added that a larger share of borrowers gravitated to ARM loans. The ARM share of activity accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year, Kan noted.

“At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week. Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%,” he said.

The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% of total applications from 41.1% the previous week. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.5% of total applications.

By product, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) share of total applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) share decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5% from the week prior.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($832,750 or less) increased to 7.38% from 7.35%. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with jumbo loan balances decreased to 7.29% from 7.31%.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages backed by the FHA decreased to 7.05% from 7.06% while rates for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages increased to 6.79% from 6.64%. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs slightly increased to 6.39% from 6.38%.

Xactus’s Mortgage Intent Index — which analyzes aggregated, anonymized credit-pull activity across the Xactus Intelligent Verification Platform — increased week-over-week to a reading of 97.8.

“Mortgage intent edged up approximately 2.2% week over week,” said Thomas Lloyd, chief strategy officer at Xactus. “The uptick follows last week’s Veterans Day-suppressed reading, suggesting underlying borrower demand remains present even in a challenging rate environment.”

Lloyd continued, “Early readings from the Daily Xactus Mortgage Intent Index offer some cautious optimism heading into Thanksgiving week — Monday’s reading of 65.9 reflects expected seasonal softness, but the year-over-year gap of approximately 16.5% is a notable improvement from the roughly 25% deficit seen in recent weeks.”

#5292. Epique’s ‘Power Agent’ trademark fight could put its branding at risk

Darryl Davis Seminars and Darryl Davis will face Epique Realty in SDNY next week over alleged POWER AGENT® trademark infringement. The court will hear a preliminary injunction motion as Epique presses counterclaims over “power” related marks.  AI Summary

Darryl Davis Seminars Inc.’s multi-million dollar federal trademark infringement lawsuit against Epique Realty, which accuses the virtual brokerage of unlawfully using the POWER AGENT® brand in its nationwide operations, is headed to court next week.

During the first week of December, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York will hold a hearing on a motion for a preliminary injunction filed by Darryl Davis and his firm that would bar Epique Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, from using the POWER AGENT trademark.

Originally filed in late June, the lawsuit alleges that Houston-based Epique Realty adopted the POWER AGENT name and “built an entire brand architecture around it” despite being put on notice and asked to stop, according to the announcement. In addition to Epique Realty, the lawsuit also lists Joshua Miller, Janice Delcid, Christopher Miller, XYZ Corps 1-10 and John and Jane Does 1-10 as defendants.

Darryl Davis Seminars says it has used the POWER AGENT mark continuously since 1993 through The POWER Program, which it describes as the real estate industry’s oldest and longest-running agent training and coaching platform.

“POWER AGENT® has been our name since 1993, and both it and THE POWER PROGRAM® are registered trademarks,” Davis told HousingWire. “The law expects a trademark owner to protect its marks. We have for decades, and we will keep doing so. Because the matter is pending, I will let our court filings speak to the rest.”

In October, Epique filed a counterclaim asking for a ruling from the court that Davis’s trademark registrations of Power Agent programs do not give his firm exclusive rights to the word “power” and that this does not give Davis or his company the rights to a family of “Power” trademarks. Epique is also asking the court to force Davis and his firm to prove likely confusing for each expression of “Power” Epique was accused of. Epique is also seeking rulings from the court that its current uses of PowerFlex and PowerCon, do not infringe on Davis’s trademarks and that it is not liable “merely because an independently controlled agent or third party used POWER-formative wording.”

Epique emphasized in the filing that its agents are independent contractors and that the company does not hold passwords for agents’ personal social media accounts in order to edit or delete content, nor does it review agents’ social media posts or websites before they are published. This contradicts Davis’s complaint, which alleges that the brokerage’s independent contractor agreement requires agents to submit marketing or advertising posts for approval prior to publication. Additionally, the company said that under state law in Texas, where Epique is headquartered, the firm is only responsible for ensuring that advertising content produced by agents complies with state rules.

In a filing earlier this month, Davis largely denied Epique’s counterclaims, namely that he is trying to trademark the word “Power” by itself and he and his firm rejected Epique’s request that the court declares that Darryl Davis Seminars does not own the word “power” exclusively and that it does not have an across-the-board monopoly over trademarks containing the word. Throughout the filing, Davis maintained that Epique infringed on his firm’s trademarks and he asked the court to reject Epique’s counter claims.

This news was first reported by Inman. Epique Realty did not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

#5291. Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

Identity security company 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

According to the company, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is said to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”

The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company says, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Beyond the customer records, the attacker is said to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the company claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

The tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. Users with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, said to be a small number, have been notified directly.

As a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning users to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

This is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the company said that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will update its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

#5290. New-Home Sales See Welcome Shift, but Not an Overall Improvement

With housing construction continuing to face supply chain and affordability challenges, the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development saw new-home sales experience a welcome shift upward.

New-home sales jumped 14.2% in October to a rate of 701,000, up from a revised rate of 614,000 in September (originally 676,000). This was also up 7.5% year-over-year.

While a positive shift for the construction industry, the shift is notably due entirely to growth in the South. While all three other regions were down both month-over-month and year-over-year to varying degrees, the South was up 36.2% month-over-month and 24.7% year-over-year.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis, noted that while any increase in new-home sales is “encouraging,” it is “too early to interpret the gain as a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

“Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices continue to limit purchasing power, and the outlook for new home sales remains sensitive to financing costs and broader economic conditions,” she continued.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant noted that as mortgage rates remain near a three-year high, “the new home industry is experiencing the same pullback in demand that we are seeing on the resale side.”

“While home builders can help offset some of the pain of higher rates by offering buyers rate buydowns and favorable financing, prospective buyers are cautious as we head into the end of 2026,” she continued. “Some buyers have been priced out of the market, while others are simply waiting until 2027, hoping for more favorable conditions.”

Inventory remained on the downslope, falling 1.5% month-over-month and 4.1% year-over-year to 477,000. At the current sales rate, this clocked in at an eight-month supply, down 14% from last month and 11.1% year-over-year.

Builder activity has been significantly diminished due to aforementioned market challenges, with builder confidence recently tanking to a 14-year low.

“Builders are responding with incentives and pricing adjustments, but a more sustained improvement in affordability will be important for strengthening housing demand,” noted NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.

In line with this trend, the median price for a new home slipped 0.3% month-over-month and 3.2 year-over-year to $391,300. Sturtevant noted that this was near a “five year low.”

“Traditionally, new homes command a premium over existing homes, but in October, the median price of a new home was 6% lower than the median price of an existing home,” she continued.”

Sturtevant concluded that with incentives and lower pricing on the table, “new homes continue to be an attractive option for buyers who remain in the market, particularly when builders can offer a discounted interest rate.”

She noted, though, that the issue at hand is “that there are simply fewer buyers in the market as we head into the last few weeks of the year.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.
