#5230. I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I paid my team a cash bonus for hitting a video target. Complaints rose, and cancellations hit 13%. Here is what the data showed and what fixed it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

For a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

We traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

When we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. New editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

That changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

Bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

We stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

The results came quickly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

The difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

We’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

The early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

While the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

If you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

#5228. DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us

Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table. With nearly 48 million Americans experiencing food insecurity in recent years, including 14 million children, millions of Americans will be facing a Thanksgiving table that has less on it.

No single organization can close this gap. It will take food banks, businesses, neighbors and public leaders all showing up.

At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever. Hunger exists in every county, and increasingly often among those who never expected to need food assistance before. More than eight in ten people surveyed by Feeding America identified rising costs as the primary driver of food insecurity.

The pressure is building for those in need. Recent changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the nation’s largest federal nutrition assistance program, have contributed to a significant decline in participation. According to the Food Research Action Center, approximately 5.5 million people have lost access to SNAP benefits since last year.

Food banks and pantries have always been the country’s backstop. But now, like everyone else in this economy, they are being asked to do more with less. Organizations are bracing demand rivalling or surpassing experienced during last fall’s government shutdown that created unprecedented disruption to SNAP. Some food banks are experiencing demand levels exceeding the COVID-19 pandemic.

Getting food to people can be just as challenging as securing it. Many of those served by food banks — including seniors, people with disabilities, or those without reliable transportation — cannot easily get to a distribution site on their own.

Tackling this challenge requires everyone contributing what they do best. For DoorDash, that’s logistics, and closing the gap between food and the people who need it.

Through Project DASH, DoorDash transports goods from food banks and pantries to doorsteps. Since 2018, 9 million deliveries of an estimated 150 million meals across the U.S. and Canada have arrived via DoorDash.

This holiday season, we’re waiving fees for more than 300 Project DASH partners between Thanksgiving and Christmas, supporting delivery of an estimated 2 million meals. By removing that expense, food bank partners can plan larger holiday distributions with confidence and reach more people.

Many of our grocery partners are also doing everything they can to make the holidays more affordable for Americans who are struggling to get by, such as offering discounts for SNAP users to stretch their budgets further. The data is clear: Making it easier to use SNAP benefits can also have a significant impact in the fight against hunger. Since introducing SNAP payments on our platform in 2023, more than 4.5 million consumers have added their SNAP cards to DoorDash, and nearly a third of those we surveyed said it has helped make them less likely to run out of food.

This is only one incremental step in a larger national conversation about hunger. No single company, program, or nonprofit can solve it alone. Food banks understand their neighbors and the needs of their communities, and businesses can bring their resources, technology, and expertise to bear.

Hunger is a neighbor-helping-neighbor issue. Americans of every background can agree that no one should go without a meal, especially at the holidays.

There is enough food for everyone in America. What’s missing is a way to get it to every table. With everyone at the table, we can build toward that together.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Daniel Riff is the head of global food access programs at DoorDash, overseeing the company’s Project DASH initiative to provide home delivery logistics for food banks, pantries and other social impact organizations. He works with government agencies, nonprofits and healthcare partners to expand meal and grocery delivery for seniors, families and individuals facing transportation barriers. He previously worked for the City of Chicago in the Mayor’s Office, where he served on the Innovation Delivery Team. DoorDash is named in this piece, and Project DASH is a DoorDash program.

#5225. American Express is giving away $1.3 million in cash to British small business owners—with no strings attached

As AI threatens to wipe out jobs, millions of people are ditching the 9-to-5 to build something of their own. And American Express is backing them with £1 million (about $1.3 million) in support to grow their small business—no strings attached.The $209 billion financial services giant is handing out £10,000 (about $13,000) grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses, in partnership with Be the Business, a U.K. organisation that helps small businesses boost their productivity.“We know that even a relatively modest investment can make a meaningful difference,” Hannah Lewis, country manager at American Express U.K., said, while adding that founders can use the cash towards “revamping their premises, reaching more customers or bringing something new to their community.”

In turn, helping them grow could help their local communities too. According to the scheme, one of the main objectives is “to help small businesses contribute to vibrant destinations, active high streets and socially connected local communities.”

Amex’s own research found that 75% of British consumers believe small businesses positively impact their local communities, and around two-thirds would be more likely to shop with a business that employs local people.

But there’s a catch: the cash can’t go toward just anything, and 5% is held back until winners prove how they spent it.

To apply, you’ll need to run an independent, for-profit business with a valid Company Registration Number, incorporated on or before Dec. 1, 2025.

You also need at least one employee on top of the owners or directors, and no more than 49 full-time equivalents. And you must operate from a permanent physical location in the U.K. that’s open to customers.

That rules a lot out. Online-only and home-based businesses, franchises, and anyone not registered with Companies House can’t apply.

But, of course, the cash comes with conditions. Winners get 95% (£9,500) once they’ve signed a grant agreement and submitted an approved budget and delivery plan. The last £500 only comes after they file a final impact report and proof of how they spent it.

The money must also go on a specific project, like shopfront improvements, accessibility upgrades, equipment, e-commerce, digital marketing, product development or community events. It can’t cover day-to-day costs such as wages, rent, or stock. Applications will be judged on business impact, community impact, and project quality and feasibility.

Amex isn’t the only company throwing money at people who want to be their own boss.

Earlier this year, Zoom gave away $150,000 to five solopreneurs in the U.S. “This isn’t about building billion-dollar companies,” Zoom’s chief marketing officer Kim Storin told Fortune. “It’s about building sustainable, profitable businesses that support a life.”

Multimillionaire entrepreneur Tim Armoo similarly launched the Legon Fund earlier this year, where he committed £5 million (around $6.7 million) of his own cash to fund AI startups founded by minority entrepreneurs.

It comes as more than 33 million Americans are self-employed, with 82% of small businesses operating without a single employee, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Meanwhile, in the U.K., there are around 1.2 million startups, with 832,000 new company incorporations registered in 2025 alone. And that number just keeps growing.

LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero told Fortune that “founder” is now one of the fastest-growing job titles on the platform, up 70% year on year.

As Armoo said, it’s never been easier to start your own business. “So now, you have no excuse, because you can learn—ChatGPT and Claude are virtually free—and if you’ve got something that’s working, here’s the money to get more customers for it.”

Orianna Rosa Royle is the Success associate editor at Fortune, overseeing careers, leadership, and company culture coverage. She was previously the senior reporter at Management Today, Britain's longest-running publication for CEOs.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin bounced back toward $60,000 this morning after news on hotter-than-expected US inflation broke and sent the crypto tumbling to $57,300, its lowest level in more than two years. The rebound has brought back speculation that Bitcoin may finally be approaching a bottom, but ETF outflows and bearish signals continue to cloud the outlook.

October’s Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation came in at 3.8% annually, while core PCE reached 3.3%, above the 3.2% expected by economists. These figures strengthened concerns that the Federal Reserve could keep monetary policy restrictive for longer, which then adds pressure to risk assets like Bitcoin.

Bitcoin nevertheless recovered after briefly dipping below $58,000, as we gauge and predict its next move.

Bitcoin remains down 23% this November, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since June 2022. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have also suffered nearly $5 billion in net outflows this month through November 24, adding another source of selling pressure.

BlackRock’s IBIT has accounted for more than $4 billion in redemptions during the month, showing how quickly institutional demand has reversed.

However, not all investors are moving in the same direction. Data cited by Nansen shows wallets that rarely move Bitcoin received a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month, while ETFs collectively sold 70,000 BTC during November.

Nansen data shows large, infrequently moving wallets absorbed a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month.Meanwhile, spot Bitcoin ETFs sold 70,000 BTC in November.The imbalance is stark. Long term cold wallets are still accumulating, but nowhere near enough to offset…

Bitcoin’s rebound also comes after an arguably huge derivatives-market reset, with leveraged positions being flushed out during the recent slide. That could reduce some immediate selling pressure.

Holders have realized $8.4 billion in net losses over the past 30 days, according to CryptoQuant data, as investors are increasingly capitulating during the selloff. But the figure remains well below the $30 billion recorded during February’s bottom and $18.4 billion during June’s low. Selling pressure has intensified, but the scale of realized losses has yet to match previous capitulation events.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Some analysts believe Bitcoin’s recovery could be running ahead of the underlying market conditions. CoinMarketCap research head Alice Liu warned that the rebound may largely reflect short sellers covering positions, and not fresh demand, leaving prices vulnerable once that buying subsides.

Meanwhile, 10x Research’s bearish signal issued in October correctly anticipated Bitcoin’s decline toward $57,300. The firm has cautioned that oversold conditions can trigger short-term rebounds without necessarily signaling a reversal in the wider trend.

“Bitcoin has reached our $57,300 target. Short-term indicators were oversold for much of the decline, and tactical bounces were always possible. Our market structure work, however, kept pointing to a bearish primary trend.” – 10X Research

Bitcoin faces a difficult combination of persistent ETF withdrawals, uncertain news from Federal Reserve policy, and weakened market sentiment. The selloff has removed substantial leverage, but convincing evidence of renewed demand remains limited.

The $57,300 low is now a key level to defend. Holding that support while ETF outflows begin slowing will likely strengthen the case that Bitcoin is forming a bottom.

#5221. Sephora’s U.S. CEO initially turned down an entry-level job at the company because she could only wear black, white, or gray to the office

In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO. Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

“I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this company called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”

“Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”

“And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.”

Patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks.

DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and quickly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

“They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.”

Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and said this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams.

“I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5219. Why hiring neurodivergent talent isn’t enough, and what leaders should do instead

Many neuroinclusion strategies still depend on employees disclosing a diagnosis. Jonathan Mok argues support should be built into how organizations operate.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

Companies are increasingly recognizing the value of neurodivergent talent, but hiring is only part of the picture. Many neuroinclusion strategies still rely on employees to disclose their diagnoses and request workplace adjustments themselves, an approach that assumes they feel safe doing so. According to a 2026 survey by the nonprofit Understood.org, about 70% of neurodivergent employees in the U.S. worry that disclosing their neurodivergence could negatively affect them at work. When employees stay silent, employers may never learn which barriers need addressing.

Jonathan Mok, a Hong Kong-based neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer, has seen that gap from both sides. He was diagnosed with ADHD and autism at 37, after years of working in education in Hong Kong. Today, he trains corporate teams across Asia on neuroinclusion and coaches executives who have received late diagnoses. His own experience suggests that even when employees do disclose, formal support does not always translate into belonging.

Jonathan Mok, neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer.

After his diagnosis, a workplace medical committee recommended that Mok should not feel obliged to attend department social gatherings. When his boss invited the team to a New Year lunch and he raised his hand to join, colleagues kept telling him nobody was forcing him to go. They meant well, but a measure intended to protect him left him feeling excluded. “I wanted to go. My boss was paying for lunch,” Mok recalls. “But the message I kept hearing was that I didn’t really belong there.”

Despite receiving formal accommodations, Mok continued to face challenges at work, and he resigned in 2020. His experience reflects a wider pattern. In a 2025 report by Boston Consulting Group, supported by SG Enable, 62% of neurodivergent employees surveyed in Singapore said their neurodivergence had been misunderstood as a poor attitude. While 99% believed reasonable accommodations would help, only 33% said these were available at their workplace, and just 24% considered them adequate.

The findings point to a disconnect between recognizing neurodivergent talent and creating the conditions for it to thrive. Gartner predicted in 2023 that by 2027, a quarter of Fortune 500 companies would actively recruit neurodivergent talent to improve business performance. Recruitment, however, is only the first step. Inclusion also depends on whether employees feel they belong, can speak up without fear of judgment, and receive support that works in practice.

Mok believes that an emphasis on meritocracy can lead some employers to assume that anyone capable enough to be hired does not need to disclose anything. Employees, in turn, try to fit in until they no longer can. He adds that organizations often focus on deficits and rely heavily on medical guidance rather than on what individuals actually want or need. In his view, support should not depend on employees asking for it; it should be built into how the organization operates.

He also challenges the idea that organizations must be ready to hire neurodivergent employees before taking any steps toward inclusion. One cosmetics retailer found that quiet shopping hours did little to ease the sensory demands of a busy store. After consulting Mok, a colleague, and store staff, it introduced ribbon-marked baskets that let customers signal a preference for minimal interaction without explaining their needs. Because retail turnover is high, the accompanying staff training was kept simple enough to pass on to new employees.

Mok points to a neurodivergent internship program at the Hong Kong office of an international insurer as a more comprehensive example. Rather than treating recruitment as the endpoint, the company paired the program with manager training and structured onboarding, helping teams build the skills to support neurodivergent colleagues. It also works with a local nonprofit organization to source talent and provide training.

To help organizations turn good intentions into action, Mok uses a 4P framework covering People, Place, Policy, and Program. It is designed as an ongoing approach rather than a one-time training session. Under People, he encourages organizations to recognize inclusive managers, create safe channels for raising concerns, and highlight neurodivergent role models. Under Place, he recommends sensory-friendly workspaces and normalizing tools that allow people to work in ways that suit them.

Policy involves clear procedures around disclosure, workplace adjustments, and job expectations, so that employees and managers know what support is available. Many managers, Mok notes, only look for guidance after a problem arises and then have to dig through documents that can run 50 or 60 pages. The program focuses on long-term planning, consultation, and partnerships with community organizations, including neurodivergent individuals and their families, so that initiatives address real needs rather than assumptions.

For companies operating across Asia, Mok stresses the importance of understanding how culture, law, and local knowledge shape neurodiversity in each market. Even within the region, conditions such as autism and ADHD are recognized differently, as the contrast between Hong Kong and mainland China shows. Such differences can complicate standardized inclusion policies. He also believes that meaningful progress is possible for organizations of every size, not only multinational corporations.

For Mok, the next stage of neuroinclusion means looking past whether organizations are willing to hire neurodivergent people and asking whether their cultures, policies, and leadership allow those employees to stay and succeed. “The next diversity metric should not be hires,” he says. “It should be stays.” A seat at the New Year lunch, offered without hesitation, may say more about an organization’s inclusion than any recruitment target.

#5218. Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users

Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in users, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, said Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she said, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the new era of online information gathering.

In their first year on Reddit, users tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune. The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have users who have over a decade of karma,” Wong said. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in this incredible way. If you look at the chart, it’s very consistent.”

Wong sees users’ changing life stages reflected in the communities they join: “[They’ve] gone through life with Reddit. You started as a student, you got your first rental place, you got married, you had kids, and we see kind of your life’s journey.

“You just never age out of Reddit because all of those life stages are available to you on Reddit, and you’re always going through something that you have to traverse.”

Navigating different life stages appears to be a key differentiator of the Reddit platform. In 2024, an article published in “Higher Education Research and Development” found that one in three students use Reddit for study help, ahead of TikTok at 14.9% and Instagram at 12.7%. YouTube leads the pack, with more than 90% of the 1,000 students surveyed using it for educational purposes.

The site’s leadership wants to expand on that function. In early November, Reddit launched Reddit Reviews, organizing product feedback across multiple communities to provide overall ratings.

“Logged-in users season very, very well, which is another motivation for us to say we want more logged-in users, because we want the opportunity to teach you about all these other aspects of Reddit,” Wong adds, “Not just the information and retrieval part of Reddit, but the part of Reddit that is around the connection, the communities, and the conversation.”

Every media platform needs to maintain or grow its audience. But Reddit has a unique problem: It has more than 100,000 “communities,” according to various reports, all of which have volunteer moderators. These moderators are unpaid and are not Reddit employees, instead choosing to spend their free time building their communities and ensuring the content is fit for its purpose.

But with ever-evolving channels and new voices within them, demand for experienced moderators is high—in fact, Reddit even has a dedicated page where communities can recruit volunteer moderators.

In the recruitment group, individuals are either looking for or offering moderation skills for hours a day, on a daily basis. Posts include requests for moderators in specific time zones, often for about 3 hours a day.

But Wong says even if Reddit wanted to bring its moderators in-house and pay them, they probably wouldn’t take it. While moderators are interested in earning, she said, they didn’t want strings attached: “They really like their independence from us, to be able to say, ‘This is our community, we set the rules, and this is how we want to operate.’

“Our relationship with moderators, I think, has greatly improved. I’ve been with Reddit eight, almost nine years, and where at the beginning we were not investing as much as we could in creating moderator tools and making their lives better in terms of reducing some of the repetitive work, over the last few years we’ve done a much better job also applying AI to help them with a toolkit, so that they can spend the time on the things that they really care about.”

But overall, Wong is bullish on Reddit’s long-term position in the age of AI. “Reddit is basically the taste layer of the internet. No model and no recommendation system can be good, I think, without a dash of Reddit in it, because you just don’t have the freshness of information. That adds value in so many places.”

#5215. Small businesses drive the economy. Who is financing their growth?

Small businesses drive much of U.S. job growth but often struggle to qualify for bank loans. Colin Kilgour sees an opening for private credit.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

When a business looks to expand its operations or invest in new equipment, its growth often depends on access to the right financing. Across America, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that from 2013 to 2023, small businesses contributed 55% of the country’s total net job creation. Between March 2023 and March 2024, they accounted for 88.9% of net job growth, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy. These figures highlight the important role small businesses play in supporting the economy. Yet, these small businesses that increasingly help the economy grow are the ones still struggling to get the support that they need.

According to a report released by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, small businesses account for between 43.5% and 50.7% of U.S. GDP and generated nearly $5.9 trillion in 2014, the most recent year available. This further illustrates how essential small businesses are to the broader economy of America. However, their economic importance may not always translate to easier access to financial opportunities.

Traditionally, one of the main barriers to small business lending is the regulatory requirements that govern how banks allocate their lending capital. Different types of loans carry different risks. Small businesses may be at a disadvantage, since their loans generally carry higher regulatory risk ratings than other forms of lending.

Collateral is another challenge. Many small businesses may not be equipped with the collateral banks typically require, such as commercial property, expensive equipment, or outstanding receivables. Processing these loans can also be costly. Since smaller loans often generate less revenue but require almost the same amount of work as larger loans, banks may find them less profitable to offer.

For Colin Kilgour, co-founder and principal of Kilgour Williams Capital, these challenges present an opportunity for investors within the private credit market. Through his work in credit and structured finance, Kilgour has seen how traditional lending practices can leave many small businesses neglected and disregarded.

Colin Kilgour, co-founder and principal of Kilgour Williams Capital.

He views the main challenge as helping small businesses secure the funding they need. “Many businesses need money to expand, renovate, or grow their operations, but struggle to qualify for traditional bank loans,” he says. He adds that some do not have the assets banks require as security, while others need smaller loans that banks may be less willing to provide.

Kilgour identifies these barriers as an opportunity for private credit to serve businesses that are often overlooked. He noted that relying solely on conventional lending requirements ought to be reconsidered. Private credit providers can look into assessing the business’s cash flow and ability to repay. Overall, his view is to offer another perspective that creates a potential source of financing for business owners who need capital to support their growth.

“Technology has changed how these businesses can be assessed,” he says. Kilgour points to open banking, which allows lenders to review a business’s financial activity. Modern financial technology, in addition, makes it possible to evaluate records and inspect business operations remotely. He emphasizes that technological advancement allows lenders to assess a business’s financial position remotely and more easily. These tools can help lenders make faster and more informed lending decisions.

In Kilgour’s view, loans can help fund expansion, equipment, or renovations while allowing owners to retain control of their businesses. The opportunity, however, also comes with risks. He recognizes that small businesses do not carry the same credit profiles as larger, investment-grade companies, which means lenders must account for potential losses and build diversified portfolios.

Kilgour sees these challenges as part of why the small-business private credit market still has room to grow. He believes the market may expand significantly as more business owners become aware of financing options beyond traditional banks. For him, the opportunity is not limited to large companies or major transactions. It may also lie in supporting the smaller businesses that contribute to the wider economy but have historically had fewer financing options.

“Private credit connects businesses with needed capital while opening opportunities for investors in an underserved market,” he says. In his view, investors should look beyond large corporate lending to Main Street businesses. By assessing risk carefully and finding more effective ways to provide capital, private credit can help connect underserved businesses with the financing they need to grow.

#5214. Hurt By Inflation? Here Are 13 Real-World Ways To Cut Costs In Your Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

With inflation still running hot, these simple moves can trim your business costs without slowing you down.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Inflation remains stubborn. Producer prices are now running at a 6.5% annual clip, and affordability is top of mind. Want to cut some costs in your business? Of course you do.  Try these moves.

Both ChatGPT and Claude offer connections to your bank account and credit card services. Or, if you’re nervous about that, just upload your statements.  You’ll be impressed by the number of suggestions they make to reduce your spending and better manage expenses.

I used to think canceling online subscriptions would be a big headache, and years ago it was. Not anymore. Search for “cancel my subscription on Google Play” (or Apple or Amazon), and you’ll get direct links to do it. I’m betting you and your business have subscriptions you’ve forgotten about that are eating up hundreds of dollars a year.

Every year, put your business and auto insurance policies out for a quote. Ask your AI chatbot to make suggestions too. This is not very time-consuming and can be accomplished using an administrative person in your office. We’re oftentimes too lazy to do this.  And that’s costing us.

Many of my clients have complicated, expensive coffee machines in their break rooms with a wide variety of coffees. They also stock sugar packets, teas, mini creamers, plastic stirrers and paper cups. It’s too much. Offer fewer coffees so you order less. Put out a sugar bowl, bring in a gallon of creamer and go back to ceramic mugs. Call me Scrooge, but it saves money.

NerdWallet does a great job regularly reviewing business and personal credit cards. Again, use your AI chatbot to look at your spending and tell it your preferences and you’ll get plenty of recommendations too.  Moving to a better card could earn you more points and cashback rewards then you’re getting right now. I have some clients that regularly switch back and forth.

Speaking of credit, if your business buys products on Amazon, then make sure you use one of Amazon’s credit cards for purchases.  With a Prime membership, you can earn 5% back on eligible Amazon purchases, and there’s no annual fee.

If you can’t pay off a credit card purchase right away from operations, consider using working capital or a lower-rate loan to reduce the balance. Credit card interest rates are high, so this can cut what you pay in interest significantly.

This is a very common tax move, yet so many of us ignore it. Put as much as you can into your retirement plan to lower your tax bill this year.  When you save – assuming you’re eligible – sock money into a Roth IRA or Roth 401K so your after-tax money grows tax-free.  With a Roth, there are no minimum distributions, and you can take the money out whenever you want, provided it meets certain requirements like a first-time home purchase, higher education or unreimbursed medical expenses.

Make sure your company has an HSA and contribute the max. It will reduce your tax expense and allow you to save money for future healthcare expenses.

Every square foot your inventory takes up costs you in overhead and space. Twice a year, take a hard look at your inventory and get rid of what isn’t moving. Sell it on Craigslist, eBay or Facebook Marketplace or scrap it.

Mark Cuban’s Cost Plus Drugs and Amazon Pharmacy both offer options that let businesses provide discounted prescription drugs, and they work with many popular health plans.

Set up a donor-advised fund and contribute to it this year, even if you haven’t decided which charities or nonprofits will receive the money. You take the deduction now and choose the recipients later.

I like Capital One Shopping. Add it as a browser extension for yourself and anyone else who makes purchases for your business. Whenever someone is on a shopping site, it searches for available coupons before you buy. It works about half the time, and it has saved me significant money over the years.

We can all afford the things we want — it’s just that sometimes we choose to spend our money on other things instead. That’s fine. But know that cutting back on things like travel, entertainment, subscriptions, marketing or other discretionary spending in your business (and your personal life) can help you reallocate your cash for other purposes.  You’re more in control than you think.

The 8-part series, which lists Barack and Michelle Obama as executive producers, is based on real-world events that led to the 2022 collapse of Bankman-Fried’s crypto exchange, FTX. Filmmakers regularly take liberties in order to increase dramatic impact. Veteran crypto journalist Laura Shin expressed a similar sentiment, stating “I’m just going to say it: Racism has to have played a role in how they portrayed [Zhao]. There’s no other explanation.”

Aside from the depictions of Zhao, other viewers complained that “The Altruists” wrongly portrayed Ellison as the mastermind behind a series of accounting frauds used to conceal holes in the balance sheet of FTX and of Bankman-Fried’s hedge fund, Alameda Research. #5209. Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

How to use AI to make your team more capable, not smaller.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

There is another way to implement AI. Start by asking how it can make your people more capable.

I learned this lesson long before the current AI boom. When we were building Amazon Web Services, talented engineers were spending too much time provisioning servers, configuring storage and handling infrastructure before they could get to the work they were actually there to do. By removing that friction, we gave developers more capacity to build, experiment and solve customer problems.

I saw the same principle years later with a junior attorney who spent hours researching and formatting before reaching the work that required her judgment. Generative AI could produce a first draft in minutes, giving her more time to refine the facts and shape the narrative for the client’s best outcome.

That is the opportunity leaders should look for with AI. Before calculating how many positions an efficiency gain could eliminate, ask what your people could accomplish if repetitive work stopped consuming so much of their day.

Suppose AI gives a team back 10 or 20% of its capacity. What happens to that time?

It could be the customer follow-up that keeps getting postponed, an improvement sitting in the backlog or a relationship that needs more attention. Those opportunities already exist inside most businesses. The problem is that people have been too busy with repetitive work to pursue them.

I saw this with a team of customer service agents who spent a significant portion of their day filling out forms and navigating cumbersome systems. An AI tool automated part of that process and gave them roughly an hour back each day.

Leadership could have used that hour to justify a smaller team. Instead, employees spent more time connecting with customers, strengthening relationships and solving more complex problems. AI removed work they disliked and created room for work where they could contribute more.

Retaining talent requires planning for people at the beginning of an AI initiative rather than after deployment. If leaders automate first and ask what happens to employees later, the priority is already clear.

Before introducing AI, divide the work into three categories. Some tasks contain little meaningful judgment and can be automated. Others can be accelerated by AI while still requiring human judgment. A third group should remain primarily human because relationships, creativity or judgment create the value. Then make the next decision before deploying anything. Where will the recovered capacity go?

That could mean moving people toward customer relationships, product development, higher-level analysis or other work that contributes more directly to growth. The destination will vary by organization, but leaders should know where they want people to go before technology begins changing their roles.

How you introduce AI also shapes whether employees embrace or resist it. If the first message people hear is that a tool will save 40% of their time, they may immediately wonder what leadership plans to do with that 40%.

Tell employees which frustrating work you want to reduce. Show them what they will have more time to accomplish. Explain how their roles can become more valuable as AI handles repetitive tasks.

Then demonstrate that commitment through what happens next. If employees see recovered time consistently reinvested into better work, stronger skills and new opportunities, AI starts to look like a tool they can use rather than a threat they need to survive.

Leaders can begin before buying another AI tool. Take one team and map how AI could change its work, then answer these four questions together before deployment.

1. What work should disappear? Break roles into individual tasks and identify repetitive work that consumes time without requiring significant human judgment. Focus first on removing friction rather than removing positions.

2. What human capability should grow? For every task AI can automate or accelerate, identify what employees could do with the recovered time. Look for work involving customers, relationships, creativity, problem-solving or judgment.

3. Where will the recovered capacity go? Give those hours a destination before deployment. If AI saves a team eight hours each week, decide whether those hours will go toward customer service, innovation, new revenue opportunities or another measurable priority.

4. What will you tell employees? Explain what AI will take off their plates and what you want them doing more of as a result. Managers should be able to describe that future clearly before asking employees to adopt the technology.

AI will change jobs, and some roles will change significantly as companies redesign how work gets done. But leaders still control a critical decision about what they do with the capacity AI creates.

Before treating efficiency as a reason to reduce headcount, ask what your people could accomplish with the time they get back. The companies that answer that question first have an opportunity to use AI for something far more valuable than cutting costs. They can use it to build a more capable workforce.

When a company announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.
